subtopics.title: Origin and observance of National Technology Day
subtopics.summary: National Technology Day is observed on 11 May each year. It was declared by PM Atal Bihari Vajpayee in 1998 to commemorate technological achievements of 11 May 1998, and has been observed annually from 1999 onward. The 2026 observance carried the theme 'Responsible Innovation for Inclusive Growth'.
facts: National Technology Day is observed on 11 May every year.
PM Atal Bihari Vajpayee declared 11 May as National Technology Day in 1998.
It has been observed annually as National Technology Day from 1999 onward.
It commemorates major technological achievements of 11 May 1998.
The 2026 observance theme was 'Responsible Innovation for Inclusive Growth'.
On 11 May 1998, Pokhran-II nuclear tests (Operation Shakti) were conducted.
On the same day, Hansa-3 completed its first successful test flight.
On the same day, DRDO successfully test-fired the Trishul short-range surface-to-air missile.
Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar awards are announced annually on National Technology Day.

subtopics.title: Pokhran nuclear tests (1974 and 1998)
subtopics.summary: India conducted a series of nuclear tests at the Pokhran Test Range in Rajasthan's Thar Desert in May 1998, under the codename Shakti. The series began on 11 May with three tests and was followed on 13 May by two more. These were the first confirmed nuclear detonations since the 1974 Pokhran-I test, codenamed 'Smiling Buddha'.
facts: Pokhran-I, India's first nuclear test, was conducted on 18 May 1974.
Pokhran-I was codenamed 'Smiling Buddha'.
Pokhran-II was a series of nuclear tests conducted by India in May 1998 at Pokhran Test Range.
The Pokhran Test Range is in Rajasthan's Thar Desert.
On 11 May 1998, India conducted three nuclear tests under the codename Shakti.
On 13 May 1998, India conducted two more nuclear tests.
Pokhran-II marked India's first confirmed nuclear detonations since the 1974 'Peaceful Nuclear Explosion'.
Operation Shakti marks India's emergence as a nuclear weapons state.
India became the 6th country to join the nuclear club.
Abdul Kalam and R. Chidambaram were the chief coordinators of Pokhran-II.

subtopics.title: Space and defence milestones
subtopics.summary: India's space and defence milestones include lunar, Mars and solar missions, along with indigenous naval and air platforms. Chandrayaan-3 achieved a soft landing near the Moon's South Pole, a global first. Upcoming missions include Gaganyaan (2027) as the first crewed spaceflight and Shukrayaan (2028) as a Venus orbiter.
facts: Chandrayaan-1 (2008) was India's first lunar mission and discovered water on the Moon.
Mangalyaan (2013) was India's first successful Mars mission, achieved on its first attempt.
In 2017, 104 satellites were launched in one launch, a world record.
Chandrayaan-3 (2023) achieved a soft landing near the Moon's South Pole, a global first.
Aditya-L1 (2023) is India's first solar mission.
Gaganyaan (2027) is the upcoming first crewed spaceflight.
Shukrayaan (2028) is the upcoming Venus Orbiter Mission.
INS Kalvari (1967) was India's first indigenous submarine.
INS Arihant is India's first ballistic missile nuclear submarine.
INS Vikrant (2022) is India's first indigenous aircraft carrier.
Tejas (LCA) is an indigenous supersonic fighter jet.

subtopics.title: Digital, farm and ranking milestones
subtopics.summary: The day also highlights India's digital infrastructure and farm milestones. Aadhaar and UPI are cited as major digital achievements, while the Green and White Revolutions transformed agriculture and dairy. India's standing in the Global Innovation Index 2026 and other rankings completes the picture.
facts: Aadhaar is the world's largest biometric ID system.
UPI (Unified Payments Interface) revolutionised digital payments.
The Green Revolution boosted production with high-yielding wheat and rice varieties.
The White Revolution made India the world's largest milk producer.
India was ranked 38th globally in the Global Innovation Index 2026.
India holds 6th position worldwide in intellectual property filings (WIPO report).
India ranks as the 3rd largest startup ecosystem globally.

subtopics.title: Institutions, schemes and awards
subtopics.summary: Several bodies and schemes support technology in India. The Technology Development Board is a statutory body that promotes the commercialisation of indigenous technology. The Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar awards, India's science honours, are announced on National Technology Day.
facts: The Technology Development Board is a statutory body under the Technology Development Board Act, 1995.
The TDB promotes development and commercialisation of indigenous technology.
The TDB also supports adaptation of imported technology for wider application.
The TDB provides financial assistance to commercialise indigenous technologies.
Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar is India's science honour, comparable to the Padma Awards.
Atal Innovation Mission, launched by NITI Aayog, fosters an innovation culture.
Atal Tinkering Labs are innovation labs in schools; Atal Incubation Centres support startups.
NM-ICPS promotes R&D in AI, Robotics, IoT, Quantum Computing and related fields.
The National Quantum Mission focuses on quantum computing, communication, sensing and materials.
iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence) promotes indigenous defence startups and MSMEs.

quizzes.passage: National Technology Day is observed in India on 11 May each year. It is a day set aside to commemorate major technological achievements, and it recalls a series of milestones the country reached on one particular date. Those milestones spanned different areas of work. One was related to nuclear research, one to aviation, and one to defence development carried out by a national research organisation. The day was given formal recognition by a senior national leader, and it has been observed every year since the first full year of observance. The name of the day has remained the same since it was first observed. Because it falls on a fixed date, the day gives the public a regular occasion to look back at how science and engineering have contributed to the country. The observance does not celebrate a single invention. Instead, it groups several achievements together under one date and one name. The milestones belonged to the same period of work, which is why they are remembered together. Each year the day keeps these achievements in the national calendar, linking past progress with present interest in technology. Its origins therefore lie in a specific set of events rather than in a general idea of progress alone.

quizzes.passage: National Technology Day is an observance in India that recognises technological achievement. It is based on a set of milestones that the country reached on one day, and the observance was created to remember them. The occasion is observed every year, and it has been part of the national calendar since its early years. The achievements it recalls belong to different fields of work. Some were linked to nuclear research, some to flight and some to the development of missiles. The observance does not celebrate one invention alone. Its name has stayed the same since the first observance, and the day is treated as a fixed point on the calendar. A national leader of the time gave the day its formal status, which is why the observance is linked to a specific decision rather than a general idea. Another part of the day's background involves the national awards for science, which are announced on the occasion. The day therefore brings together several strands: a historical date, a list of technical milestones, a formal decision by a leader, and a regular annual observance that keeps these achievements in view for the public. Each observance returns attention to the same set of achievements.

quizzes.passage: National Technology Day also draws attention to India's progress in digital infrastructure, farm output and dairy. These achievements are not limited to laboratories. They affect how citizens pay for goods, how farmers grow food and how milk reaches households. The observance groups these areas together with the country's scientific and engineering work. International assessments also compare countries on innovation, patents and intellectual property, and these comparisons are published by global bodies. Such assessments are referred to in discussions about the country's technological standing. The observance therefore links everyday technology with national standing. Each year, the day offers a chance to look at these developments together, including the systems that run across the country and the changes in food and dairy production. These achievements show how technology has entered ordinary life. They form a second strand of the observance, alongside the milestones that the day recalls from its origin. The areas are varied, which is why the day is treated as a broad recognition of technological progress rather than of one sector alone. Their scope is one reason the observance is wider than a single anniversary of one event. Taken as a whole, the observance covers machines, laboratories, farms and dairies alike.

Digital systems now reach large numbers of people in their everyday lives, and the observance treats them as a major area of progress. Farm output and dairy production have also changed over several decades, and these changes are placed alongside the country's scientific work. Several indices and reports from global bodies are used to discuss how the country performs in innovation and intellectual property. Such reports are referred to in discussions about technological standing, and they are part of the wider picture the observance describes. The day therefore brings together technology in daily life with national performance in research. Its framework covers machines, laboratories and the systems that serve citizens directly. Each year, the day gives the public an occasion to review these areas together and to consider the progress they represent. quizzes.passage: India runs a number of public bodies, missions and schemes that are meant to support technology. These institutions differ in their purpose. Some work on research and development, some support new companies, and some focus on the link between government needs and private innovation. A few programmes are designed for students, so that young people can take part in experiments and build practical skills early in their education. Others target specialised sectors where the country wants to develop its own capabilities. Some bodies were created by a specific Act, while others operate as programmes under national agencies. Some are led by national bodies, while others operate through government departments. Support can take the form of funding, training, facilities or access to expert networks. Together these arrangements form a support system that links science, industry and education. Each institution has its own role within this system. Some schemes are linked to national missions with defined focus areas. The variety of these arrangements is one reason the day is observed as a broad recognition of technological work. This variety is visible in the range of programmes that the country runs at once, in several sectors. Each of them can be understood by its purpose, its sector and the group it serves.

quizzes.passage: India supports technology through a mix of statutory bodies, national missions and smaller programmes. Some of these arrangements are created by a specific law, while others come from national planning bodies that set priorities for innovation. Schemes aim to help research reach the market, to encourage new ideas among young people and to build capacity in areas such as defence technology and emerging sciences. Support can come in the form of money, training, facilities or access to expert networks. Some bodies are directed at industry, others at schools and universities, and some work across several areas at once. The national awards for science also form part of this landscape. Each of these bodies has its own focus and its own method of working. The overall picture is one of institutions that complement one another, each with a defined area of work, and that together aim to strengthen national technological capability. Students, researchers and entrepreneurs are among the groups that these programmes are designed to reach. The range of these programmes shows how technology policy in India covers education, research, industry and defence at the same time. Students and schools form one part of this effort, while defence and space form another.
